Throughout the course we use ethical dilemmas — short scenarios with no
clean answer — as a way to practice moral reasoning. The point is never to
find the correct choice. It is to notice why a situation feels hard, to
name the values that pull against each other, and to hear how classmates weigh
those values differently.

Some of these dilemmas are drawn from philosophy (Plato, the trolley problem),
some from psychology experiments, and some from real events. As you read one,
it can help to ask:

  • Who is affected by each option, and how?
  • Which ethical framework (consequences, duties, virtues, care) does my gut reaction lean on?
  • What would change my mind?

There are no grades attached to any position you take here — only to the care
you bring to reasoning it through.

For more on why sitting with uncertainty is a feature rather than a bug, see George Saunders on the value of not knowing.
